name: BETADIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: A
args.about: the lowest value (0 if left out)

args.name: B
args.about: the highest value (1 if left out)

about: Gives the chance of a value up to x in a beta spread.

example.why: For a beta spread with alpha 2 and beta 3, the chance of 0.4 or less is 0.5248.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use BETA.DIST instead. It always gives the cumulative chance.

name: HYPGEOMDIST

args.name: sample_s
args.about: how many successes in the sample

args.name: population_s
args.about: how many successes in the whole group

args.name: number_pop
args.about: the size of the whole group

about: Gives the chance of exactly so many successes when drawing without putting back.

example.why: Drawing 4 balls from 20 with 8 red, the chance of exactly 1 red is about 0.363.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use HYPGEOM.DIST instead.

name: LOGNORMDIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out it is, above 0

about: Gives the chance of a value up to x when its logarithm follows a bell curve.

example.why: ln 4 is 1.386, which is 1.76 spreads below 3.5, so the chance is about 0.039.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use LOGNORM.DIST instead. It always gives the cumulative chance.

name: NEGBINOMDIST

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success each time

about: Gives the chance of so many failures before a number of successes.

example.why: With a 1 in 4 chance each time, the chance of exactly 10 failures before the 5th success is about 0.055.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use NEGBINOM.DIST instead.

name: NORMSDIST

args.name: z
args.about: how many spreads from the average

about: Gives the chance of a value up to z on the standard bell curve.

example.why: 84% of the standard bell curve lies below 1.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use NORM.S.DIST instead.

name: TDIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, a whole number

args.name: tails
args.about: 1 for one tail, 2 for both tails

about: Gives the chance of a t value beyond x, in one or both tails.

example.why: With 60 degrees of freedom, the chance of a t further from 0 than 1.96 is about 0.055.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use T.DIST.2T or T.DIST.RT instead.

name: BETAINV

args.name: A
args.about: the lowest value (0 if left out)

args.name: B
args.about: the highest value (1 if left out)

about: Gives the value with a given chance below it in a beta spread.

example.why: In a beta spread with alpha 2 and beta 3, 52.48% lies below 0.4.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use BETA.INV instead.

name: BINOMDIST

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success each time

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the chance of exactly x

about: Gives the chance of so many successes in a number of tries.

example.why: Tossing a coin 10 times, the chance of exactly 6 heads is 210/1024.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use BINOM.DIST instead.

name: CHIDIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, a whole number

about: Gives the chance of a chi-squared value above x (the right tail).

example.why: With 10 degrees of freedom, 5% of chi-squared values are above 18.307.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use CHISQ.DIST.RT instead.

name: CHIINV

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, a whole number

about: Gives the chi-squared value with a given chance above it.

example.why: With 10 degrees of freedom, 5% of chi-squared values are above 18.307.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use CHISQ.INV.RT instead.

name: CHITEST
about: Tests whether counts you saw differ from what you expected, giving the chance it's luck.

example.why: The gaps from the expected counts give a chi-squared of 3.57 on 2 degrees of freedom, a 17% chance.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use CHISQ.TEST instead.

name: CONFIDENCE

args.name: alpha
args.about: how much chance of being wrong, like 0.05

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out it is, above 0

about: Gives the margin either side of a sample average for a confidence interval, using the bell curve.

example.why: 1.96 × 2.5 / √50 = 0.693, so the average is within ±0.693 with 95% confidence.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use CONFIDENCE.NORM instead.

name: COVAR

args.name: array2
args.about: the second set, the same size

about: Gives how two sets of numbers vary together (population covariance).

example.why: The products of each pair's distance from its average, averaged over the 3 pairs.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use COVARIANCE.P instead.

name: CRITBINOM

args.name: probability_s
args.about: the chance of success each time

args.name: alpha
args.about: the chance to reach, between 0 and 1

about: Gives the smallest number of successes whose cumulative chance reaches alpha.

example.why: With 6 coin tosses, the chance of 4 or fewer heads is the first to reach 75%.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use BINOM.INV instead.

name: EXPONDIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the chance of exactly x

about: Gives the chance for a waiting time in an exponential spread.

example.why: At 10 an hour, the chance of waiting 0.2 hours or less is 1 − e^-2 = 0.865.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use EXPON.DIST instead.

name: FDIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: deg_freedom1
args.about: the degrees of freedom on top

about: Gives the chance of an F value above x (the right tail).

example.why: With 6 and 4 degrees of freedom, 1% of F values are above 15.2.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use F.DIST.RT instead.

name: FINV

args.name: deg_freedom1
args.about: the degrees of freedom on top

about: Gives the F value with a given chance above it.

example.why: With 6 and 4 degrees of freedom, 1% of F values are above 15.2.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use F.INV.RT instead.

name: FTEST
about: Tests whether two sets of numbers are equally spread, giving the chance it's luck.

example.why: The two spreads are close enough that the chance they differ by luck is about 65%.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use F.TEST instead. Both tails are counted.

name: GAMMADIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the chance of exactly x

about: Gives the chance for a value in a gamma spread.

example.why: In a gamma spread with alpha 9 and beta 2, the chance of 10 or less is about 0.068.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use GAMMA.DIST instead.

name: GAMMAINV
about: Gives the value with a given chance below it in a gamma spread.

example.why: In a gamma spread with alpha 9 and beta 2, 6.81% lies below 10.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use GAMMA.INV instead.

name: LOGINV

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out it is, above 0

about: Gives the value with a given chance below it when its logarithm follows a bell curve.

example.why: It undoes LOGNORMDIST: 3.9% of values lie below 4.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use LOGNORM.INV instead.

name: MODE
about: Gives the number that comes up most often.

example.why: 8 comes up three times, more than any other size.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use MODE.SNGL (or MODE.MULT for every most-common value) instead.

name: NORMDIST

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out it is, above 0

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the chance of exactly x

about: Gives the chance for a value on a bell curve with a given average and spread.

example.why: 180 is one spread above the average 170, and 84% of the curve lies below that.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use NORM.DIST instead.

name: NORMINV

args.name: standard_dev
args.about: how spread out it is, above 0

about: Gives the value with a given chance below it on a bell curve.

example.why: 90% of heights lie below 170 + 1.2816 × 10 = 182.8.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use NORM.INV instead.

name: NORMSINV
about: Gives the z value with a given chance below it on the standard bell curve.

example.why: 97.5% of the standard bell curve lies below 1.96.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use NORM.S.INV instead.

name: PERCENTILE
about: Gives the value a given share of the numbers lie below.

example.why: A quarter of the way along the sorted scores falls between 70 and 75.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use PERCENTILE.INC instead.

name: PERCENTRANK

args.name: significance
args.about: how many digits to keep (3 if left out)

about: Gives where a value stands among numbers, as a share from 0 to 1.

example.why: 75 is the 3rd of 6 scores: 2 of the 5 gaps lie below it, so 0.4.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use PERCENTRANK.INC instead.

name: POISSON

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the chance of exactly x

about: Gives the chance of so many events when they happen at random at an average rate.

example.why: With 5 calls an hour on average, the chance of exactly 2 is 5² e^-5 / 2! = 0.084.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use POISSON.DIST instead.

name: QUARTILE

args.name: quart
args.about: 0 smallest, 1 first quarter, 2 middle, 3 third quarter, 4 largest

about: Gives a quartile of a set of numbers.

example.why: The first quartile lies a quarter of the way along the sorted scores.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use QUARTILE.INC instead.

name: RANK

args.name: ref
args.about: the numbers to rank it among

args.name: order
args.about: 0 for largest first, 1 for smallest first (0 if left out)

about: Gives a number's place in a list, 1 being the largest.

example.why: Ranked smallest first, Ben's 47 comes 1st.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use RANK.EQ instead.

name: STDEVP
about: Gives how spread out numbers are, treating them as the whole group.

example.why: The average is 5 and the squared gaps average 4, whose square root is 2.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use STDEV.P instead.

name: TINV

args.name: deg_freedom
args.about: the degrees of freedom, a whole number

about: Gives the t value with a given chance beyond it in both tails.

example.why: With 60 degrees of freedom, 5% of t values are further from 0 than 2.0003.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use T.INV.2T instead.

name: TTEST
about: Tests whether two sets of numbers have different averages, giving the chance it's luck.

example.why: Paired, the gaps between Before and After could be luck about 20% of the time.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use T.TEST instead.

name: VAR
about: Gives how spread out numbers are (variance), treating them as a sample.

example.why: The squared gaps from the average 5 add up to 32; 32 / 7 = 4.571.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use VAR.S instead.

name: VARP
about: Gives how spread out numbers are (variance), treating them as the whole group.

example.why: The squared gaps from the average 5 add up to 32; 32 / 8 = 4.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use VAR.P instead.

name: WEIBULL

args.name: x
args.about: the value to work out the function at

args.name: cumulative
args.about: TRUE for the chance of up to x, FALSE for the chance of exactly x

about: Gives the chance for a value in a Weibull spread, often used for how long things last.

example.why: With shape 20 and scale 100, the chance of failing by 105 hours is about 0.93.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use WEIBULL.DIST instead.

name: ZTEST

args.name: sigma
args.about: the known spread (the sample's own if left out)

about: Gives the chance of a sample average this high or higher if the true average were x.

example.why: The sample average 5.1 is high enough above 4 to happen by luck about 9% of the time.

notes: An older name kept for old spreadsheets: use Z.TEST instead. This is one-tailed.
